seo.title: Yawn: AI Agent Operations Dashboard Case Study
seo.description: How we built Yawn, the dashboard that turns client emails into planned, built and reviewed work by AI agents, with a human approving three things per job. Built in four days, now improving itself.

caseStudy.heading: A dashboard where AI agents do the client work, and we approve three things per job.
caseStudy.intro: Pixeldev is a small studio with a lot of clients. Requests arrive by email, Messenger, ClickUp and job boards, and every one needs the same loop: read it, find the repo, plan, build, check, ship, reply. Yawn is the product we built to run that loop with AI agents, so that work keeps moving when nobody is at a desk, and nothing reaches a client without a person saying yes.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: We had already tried twice. Both earlier attempts proved that an agent could do a lot of a job, and both left real scars: agents sharing one live working tree and shipping each other's half-finished edits, a single-writer database that stalled, no push notifications, and agents so locked down that one small job needed five plan approvals. Neither could tell us, in one place, what was running, what was waiting on us and what it was costing.

The bigger cost was context. When a client replied to a job finished three weeks ago, the history of what was asked and what shipped lived in an inbox, a terminal scrollback and someone's memory. Work stalled whenever we were away from a desk, which for a studio that visits clients is most of the day.

sections.heading: What we built
paragraphs: Yawn is a single-owner operations dashboard, installed on a phone as an app and running on one server. Each client has its own context and Connections: git repos, websites with their environments, servers, mailboxes, chat channels, ClickUp, job boards and the logins for their support desks. Inbound messages on those Connections become Tasks, or attach to the Task they belong to.

Every Task is worked by real Claude Code sessions with the full toolset and the repo's own skills and rules. The Assistant drafts a Plan. A Builder does the work in its own git worktree and branch, so concurrent jobs never see each other's changes. A separate Reviewer reads the diff against the approved Plan and flags what it finds. Then it comes to us.
steps: Three decisions per Task: approve the Plan, review the work, approve the reply. Each is a card we can answer in one tap from Home, the board or a push notification.

Approvals for anything production-class. A deploy, a migration on a live server or a message to a real person pauses the agent and shows us the exact command and its effect, with Approve once, Always allow and Deny.
A Review page with what the Builder did, the checks that ran, the Reviewer's findings and the diff file by file. Click a line to comment and send it back.
A master chat that sees every Task and every agent, live and past, and can run any dashboard operation. We can type to it, talk to it, and have it answer aloud.
Intake from Gmail, IMAP mailboxes, Messenger, ClickUp and job boards, routed to the right client by sender and thread, with an Unassigned inbox for anything it can't place.
Self-improvement. Asking Yawn to change itself goes through the same Plan, build, review and merge flow, then it builds its own release, deploys it, health-checks it and rolls back on failure.

figure.alt: A Task in Review: 'Add subscription toggle to product page' for a fictional coffee roaster. The page shows what the Builder did, the client, branch and who built and checked it, and the diff of a new JavaScript file, with Send back, Re-plan and Approve and merge buttons at the top.
figure.caption: Review leads with what the Builder did and what the Reviewer found, then the diff. Approve and merge merges the branch, runs the repo's ship steps and sends the reply.

sections.heading: The hard part
paragraphs: Giving agents real power without giving them the keys. An agent working for one client must never be able to touch another client's systems, so each client's sessions run as their own OS user on the server, reach only that client's Connections, and never see a password: website logins are typed by Yawn's own browser, and a Keap or Google token is used by the API on the agent's behalf. Production-class actions are caught by a policy hook before they run, not described in a prompt and hoped for.

The other hard part was keeping work alive. Sessions are owned by a separate long-lived host process, so the API can be redeployed, including by Yawn itself, without ending a Run. If that host crashes, it reconciles what it finds on boot rather than blindly re-running: a turn that ended inside a non-read-only call becomes a failed Run that names the call, and waits for us.

It is also the first thing we have built that improves itself in production. Of its 813 commits, 52 were made by Yawn: a Builder working in a worktree of its own repo, its own test suite run before Review, a release built and deployed by its own deployer with automatic rollback. The memory limits in the deployment notes exist because two of those early self-changes swapped the server to a halt, and the fix was shipped the same way.

figure.alt: The Needs you panel on Home. One card shows a plan ready for approval with three numbered steps and Approve plan, Edit and Decline buttons. Another shows an agent paused before an SSH command that would run a database migration on a production server, explained in plain language, with Approve once, Always allow and Deny.
figure.caption: An Approval card shows the exact command and what it does. This one is a migration on a server Yawn does not know, so it counts as production and waits.

sections.heading: How it went
paragraphs: The spec, 123 user stories and a 37-screen design canvas, was written on 14 November 2026. Four days and 113 tickets later it was running our client work in production on Dokploy, with passkey sign-in, push notifications and voice. It has been taking in client email, ClickUp tasks and Messenger chats since, and we now spend our mornings approving plans and reading diffs instead of reading inboxes.

What it changed for us is the shape of a working day. A client's request arrives at 6am, a Plan is waiting by the time we look at a phone, and the work is in Review by the time we are at a desk. The history of every job lives on its Task, so when a client writes back a month later the agent starts with everything that was decided the first time. We're still adding to it, and increasingly it adds to itself.

figure.alt: The Agents page: two of three slots in use. The Builder section lists two live sessions, one on step 2 of 3 for a fictional gym and one starting a run for a freight company, each with Open, Pause and Stop. The Reviewer shows no live session and its last run. The Assistant drafts plans and does not take a slot.

asideCta.heading: Want AI agents doing real work in your business, with you in control?
asideCta.body: Yawn is what that looks like for us. Tell us what repeats in your week, and we'll tell you where an agent could take it on and where a person should stay in the loop.
